entry.title: Scrambled brains at 30 spikes/s (17 Oct 2026, our own test, pre-registered, brain only): 17 Oct: at 30 spikes/s, the weakest tested input at which the real brain's turn command appeared, we also ran 2 scrambled brains per side (each neuron keeps its number of connections; one 1-second trial each, with the same trial seed as the real-wiring body runs). On the left side, neither scrambled brain sent a turn command, and their steering signals were identical to having no brain, so in the body they walk like the no-brain fly (the real wiring turned it about 11 deg). On the right side, neither scrambled brain sent a turn command, and their steering signals were identical to having no brain, so in the body they walk like the no-brain fly (the real wiring turned it about 17 deg). As at 80 spikes/s, none of the scrambled brains we ran produced the turn; at 30 spikes/s we did not turn their activity up to match the real brain. The scrambled brains were not matched for overall activity: they fired 48% (left) and 44% (right) as many spikes as the real brain at this strength. Most of those spikes were the stimulated input neurons themselves; outside the input, the scrambled brains fired about 1% as many spikes as the real brain. These body runs turn the brain's firing rates into steering through our own hand-made mapping, so they show the brain result in degrees; they are not a separate test of the wiring. We ran scrambled brains at 30 and 80 spikes/s, not at 20, 40 or 60.

Relay update under the 13 Oct headline, which stays (17 Oct 2026; a count from the map, not a new trial): "The two sides disagree: on one side silencing the relays lowered the turn neuron's rate more than matched activity elsewhere, on the other it did not. We do not draw a conclusion." We also looked for a stricter control: other active inputs that excite the turn neuron with a similar firing rate and a similar number of connections onto it. In this model there are none for any of the active relay neurons on either side (count of 15 Oct: the busiest relay, PVLP141, fires about 100 spikes/s; no other such input fires above 43), so that stricter test cannot be built here.

Browser re-check of the six demos of 3 Oct: Re-checked 17 Oct in the same no-GPU browser: 1 of 6 ran (3 Oct: 3 of 6). Fly Worker: loaded, but showed no activity (3 Oct: ran). fly67: did not load (3 Oct: ran). Checked in headless Chromium 154 on a Linux server without a GPU, 17 Oct 2026. Shows whether the page loads, downloads its brain data and keeps computing; it is not a play test. Safari, Firefox, phones and GPU machines were not tested.

Relay update under the 13 Oct headline, which stays (15 Oct 2026, pre-registered, brain only): "The two sides disagree: on one side silencing the relays lowered the turn neuron's rate more than matched activity elsewhere, on the other it did not. We do not draw a conclusion." 15 Oct: we ran 5 more matched controls on the right side, 10 in all. Every one of them left the turn neuron's rate higher than silencing the relays did (controls 38-47 Hz, relays 25.7 Hz), so the right-side reading did not change. Our rule compares the relays with the lowest matched control, so extra controls can only make the relays look less special, never more. Right-eye matched controls: 40, 41, 41, 43, 40, 43, 47, 38, 47, 46 Hz. Counts: 5 seeds per side; 5 matched draws on the left and 10 on the right.

The looming turn in degrees, at each input strength (14 Oct 2026, our own test, pre-registered, simulated body): left eye: In the body, the fly turned away from 30 spikes/s per looming neuron upward on this side, the strength at which the brain's turn command appeared; the turn was about 11 deg at 30 and about 37 deg at 80 (our mapping turns the brain's rates into steering). Right eye: At 30 spikes/s the turn was borderline: the fly turned away in 1 of 2 runs on this side; from 40 upward it turned away in every run. The right-eye borderline rests on one run (seed 0 at 30 spikes/s, 9.18 deg against the 10 deg rule). These body runs turn the brain's firing rates into steering through our own hand-made mapping, so they show the brain result in degrees; they are not a separate test of the wiring. No scrambled brains were run at these strengths.

Body lines under the 13 Oct relay headline, which stays the headline (14 Oct 2026, descriptive, one run per arm and side): With PVLP141 silenced, the fly still turned away, by about 24 deg instead of 37 deg (one run per side; our mapping). With all 21-23 two-step relay neurons silenced, the fly still turned away, by about 37 deg instead of 37 deg (one run per side; our mapping). (left eye; unrounded 37.3 vs 37.2 deg) With PVLP141 silenced, the fly still turned away, by about 34 deg instead of 55 deg (one run per side; our mapping). (right eye) These body runs turn the brain's firing rates into steering through our own hand-made mapping, so they show the brain result in degrees; they are not a separate test of the wiring.
